Reading · living with wildlife

1.1 Discuss. Are there any wild animals near where you live? Do people welcome them, or complain about them?

KEY WORDS

to monitor to watch and measure over time

flood defences walls and pumps that control water

a drainage ditch a channel dug to drain a field

a nuisance something annoying and costly

The Beavers Are Coming Back

In 2011, a farmer in Devon reported seeing an animal in his river that had not lived wild in England for four hundred years. He was not believed. Two years later somebody filmed it, and the argument that followed was surprisingly fierce: a wild beaver had returned, nobody knew how, and the government announced that it was going to remove them.

The case for leaving them alone rested on flooding. Beavers build dams, and dams slow water down. Over the five years the Devon animals were monitored, the flow leaving their stretch of river during heavy rain fell by around thirty per cent, and the water arriving in the village downstream was measurably cleaner. Flood defences of the conventional kind — concrete, pumps, engineers — cost millions and need constant maintenance. Beavers work for nothing.

Farmers were less enthusiastic, and their objection was not unreasonable. A beaver does not distinguish between a stream that needs slowing and a drainage ditch that somebody paid to dig. Where the two interests collide, one of them loses, and it is not usually the beaver.

The government changed its mind in 2020, and the animals are now legally protected. Several counties are releasing their own populations this year, and by 2035 beavers are expected to be living in most English river systems. Whether that turns out to be a triumph or an expensive nuisance will depend almost entirely on how carefully the next decade is managed.

2

Grammar · future forms

PRESENTATION

will — a decision made now, a prediction, an offer or a promise:

I think it will rain. · That bag looks heavy — I'll carry it.

be going to — a plan decided before now, or a prediction based on evidence you can see:

We're going to plant two hundred trees. · Look at those clouds — it's going to pour.

present continuous — a fixed arrangement, usually with a time or a place: I'm meeting the council at four.

present simple — timetables: The train leaves at 6.40. · might / may — possible, not certain.

Form

Use

I'll call you later.

a decision made at the moment of speaking

We're going to build a dam.

a plan decided before now

I'm seeing the minister at two.

a fixed arrangement

The train leaves at 6.40.

a timetable

It might rain tomorrow.

possible, but not certain

ERROR WARNING

Never use will after when, as soon as, before, after, until or if:

I'll call you when I will arrive. ✗ I'll call you when I arrive. ✓

Use going to when you can see the evidence; will for an opinion:

Look at that sky — it will rain. ✗ Look at that sky — it's going to rain. ✓

shall is used mainly for offers and suggestions: Shall I help you? · Shall we start?

4

Everyday English · giving reasons, results and examples

4.1 Read the conversation.

Nodira Why did the council reject the plan?

Bekzod Mainly because of the cost, as far as I know.

Nodira But the flooding is getting worse. Last February, for example, half the main street was under water.

Bekzod Exactly. And since the trees would be far cheaper, the decision seems very strange.

Nodira So what happens now?

Bekzod Nothing, as a result. We simply wait for the next flood.

Nodira That can't be the end of it, surely.

Giving a reason

Giving a result

Giving an example

because / since / as

so / therefore

for example / for instance

because of + noun

as a result

such as

due to / owing to + noun

consequently

take …, for example

ERROR WARNING

because + clause · because of + noun:

because of the river flooded ✗ because the river flooded ✓ · because of the flooding ✓

Use one connector, not two: Because of the rain, so we stayed inside. ✗
